profile.a: Group 28 of the Cambridge Venture Project: Francisco Zubizarreta, Lei Wang, Sophie (Quynh) Nguyen and Tyler Schonewolf.
Arthur Rank Hospice Charity (ARHC), the only adult hospice in Cambridgeshire, and its acting CEO.
Why the hospice reaches far fewer non-White European patients than live in its area, and how to close the gap.
Michaelmas term 2024, using ARHC patient data from April 2023 to September 2024.
Cambridgeshire, benchmarked against hospice models in the US, UK, Singapore, Australia, India and South Africa.
Non-White European groups are about 12% of Cambridgeshire's population but only about 3.5% of ARHC's patients; religion, family values, language and low visibility of services keep them away.

Secondary research on demography, hospice data and outreach best practice; interviews with the acting CEO, GPs, matrons, staff and donors; a decision-factor synthesis, a risk register and a short- and long-term action plan.

charts.title: Who lives in Cambridgeshire and who the hospice serves (%)
charts.takeaway: The hospice over-serves White British residents and serves non-White European residents at under a third of their population share. This is the gap the whole project is about.
charts.source: Page 43. Values read from the deck's chart and approximate.

charts.title: Every minority group is under-served (% of population vs % of patients)
charts.takeaway: The shortfall is not one community: no group reaches even half its population share. The largest gaps are Other Mixed, Other Asian and Chinese residents, which argues for broad outreach rather than one targeted programme.
charts.source: Page 43. Values read from the deck's chart and approximate.

charts.title: Patients by recorded religion (%)
charts.takeaway: Religion is unknown for 59% of patients. The deck names faith as a main barrier, yet the hospice cannot see who it is missing; better data capture is a first step the recommendations do not list.

charts.title: Risk register: impact of each risk
charts.takeaway: The highest risk is perception, not operations, so the first actions are culturally sensitive campaigns and testimonials from diverse patients.

charts.title: Hospice models compared: accessibility and integration (%)
charts.takeaway: The UK model ranks near the top on both measures, so ARHC's gap is about reaching specific communities rather than a weak system. The deck does not define how the percentages were measured.

charts.title: Action plan

items.label: Simplified referral system with the NHS

charts.takeaway: Trust-building comes first and structural change second; no action has an owner, cost or measure attached.
charts.source: Page 46. The deck gives phases, not dates.

charts.title: Why patients hold back, and the answer to each

items.title: Religion and family values
items.text: 'God decides', avoidance of disclosure, caring at home. Answer: work through faith leaders and community champions.

items.title: Communication
items.text: Family members as interpreters; pain under-estimated. Answer: translators, multilingual staff and website translation.

items.title: Location and referral
items.text: Rural gaps and Hospice-at-Home bureaucracy. Answer: simpler NHS referral and satellite services.

items.title: Past experience
items.text: Racism or insensitivity in earlier care. Answer: diverse hiring and cultural competency training.

items.title: Perception
items.text: Hospice seen only as end-of-life care. Answer: early-stage pathway campaigns and personal stories.

items.title: Planning
items.text: Less advance care planning, more mistrust of carers. Answer: early identification and personalised care.
